prompt: A tester wants to know whether a product's name is in what the server sends, before any script runs. Where should she look?

choices.text: The Elements panel, which shows the page
choices.why: The Elements panel shows the DOM as it is now, after the scripts have changed it.

choices.text: View page source
choices.why: Right. The source is the file as it arrived, which answers exactly the question of what came before any script ran.

choices.text: The Console, with `document.body.innerHTML`
choices.why: The Console runs against the live DOM, so it reports the page after the script filled it.

choices.text: The Accessibility tab of the panel
choices.why: That tab shows roles and names in the current tree, not the file the server sent.

prompt: A page works on a developer's Mac and, deployed to a Linux server, draws no styles. The Network panel shows `404 GET /Style.css`. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The file is saved with a different capital letter
choices.why: Right. The Mac's disk ignored the case of the name and the Linux server does not, as with `App.js` in lesson 1.

choices.text: Linux browsers do not load stylesheets from the root
choices.why: The browser asked and the server answered 404; the browser did its part.

choices.text: The stylesheet was cached on the Mac and is missing
choices.why: A cache on the Mac cannot make the server answer 404; the server looked for the file and found none.

choices.text: The server needs `Cache-Control` on CSS
choices.why: A header describes how to keep a file the server found; this one was not found at all.

prompt: A page's HTML names one script. The script asks for `/api/user`, and only when that answers asks for `/api/orders`. Put the requests in the order the Network panel lists them.
trap: The script cannot ask for anything before it has arrived and run, and the second request waits for the first.

prompt: With the shop just reset, somebody adds two bananas and one acerola. What `total` does `GET /api/basket` answer, in the unit the shop keeps prices in?
A team upgrades Playwright past 1.56.0, and every run now stops at `Executable doesn't exist at …/chromium_headless_shell-1194/…`. They downloaded Chromium last month. What happened?

choices.text: The cache folder was emptied by the upgrade
choices.why: An upgrade of the library does not delete browsers; the old build is still on disk, it is simply not the one asked for.

choices.text: Headless runs need a separate licence
choices.why: Nothing about headless Chromium is licensed separately; the message is about a missing file.

choices.text: The new version wants another build
choices.why: Right. The build number in the path belongs to a version, and `npx playwright install chromium` fetches the one the new version expects.

choices.text: The shop is still listening on port 3000
choices.why: A busy port prints `EADDRINUSE`; this message names a browser file.

prompt: The shop's home page is opened in a window 400 pixels wide. How many elements does `button:visible` match?
A test finds the Guava's price with `//p[contains(., "2,90")]`. It matches one element today. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Nothing; one match is what a locator for one thing needs
choices.why: One match today is necessary and not enough: the expression says nothing about guavas.

choices.text: XPath cannot compare text that holds a comma
choices.why: A comma is an ordinary character to `contains`; the trouble is what else contains it.

choices.text: `contains` skips the non-breaking space and fails
choices.why: The four characters it looks for do not include the space, which is why it found the price at all.

choices.text: Any later price ending in 2,90 also matches
choices.why: Right. Like `5,90` matching R$ 15,90, it is correct only while no other price holds those characters, and a wrong match stays green.

prompt: Which of these CSS selectors match exactly one element on the shop's home page? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `[data-testid="product-mango"] small`
choices.why: Right. The descendant combinator reaches the `small` inside the price.

choices.text: `[data-testid="product-mango"] > small`
choices.why: It matches 0: the `small` is a grandchild of the card, not a child.

choices.text: `[data-testid="product-mango"] > p > small`
choices.why: Right. Two child steps, card to `p` to `small`, find the one element.

choices.text: `.card:has(small)`
choices.why: Every card has a `small`, so it matches all eight.

prompt: On the shop's home page, once the eight cards are drawn, a test runs `await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Fruit of the season')`. What happens?

choices.text: It passes, because the first heading has that text
choices.why: Playwright does not pick the first match for an assertion about one element.

choices.text: A strict mode violation: nine headings match
choices.why: Right. The `h1` and the eight card `h2`s all have the role heading, and an assertion about one element refuses to guess.

choices.text: It fails after five seconds of retrying
choices.why: A locator that matches more than one element fails at once with strict mode, without waiting out the timeout.

choices.text: It passes once `{ exact: true }` is not given
choices.why: `exact` changes how a name is matched; this locator gives no name at all, so it reaches every heading.

prompt: `getByText('Passion')` matches the card titled Passion fruit, because by default it matches part of the text. To make it match only the whole text, the option is `{ ___ : true }`.
On the search page, a robot types `guava` with no pause between keys. Using the server's rule, what does the list end on?

choices.text: Guava, 1 found
choices.why: The answer to `guava` arrives first and is replaced by every slower answer after it.

choices.text: Mango and Guava, 2 found
choices.why: Right. The answer to `g` waits longest, 750 ms, so it lands last, and two names contain a g.

choices.text: All eight fruit, because `g` matches everything
choices.why: The route keeps only names containing the letter; six names have no g.

choices.text: An empty list, since nothing has answered
choices.why: Every question is answered within 750 ms; the list is not empty at the end.

prompt: `papaya` is typed with 100 ms between keys, the first key at 0 ms. By the server's rule `max(0, 900 - 150 * length)`, and ignoring the network, at how many milliseconds does the answer to `papaya` arrive?
A test fills a search box, and only then calls `await page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes('/api/search'))`. The server answers in 3 ms. What can happen?

choices.text: The wait returns the response that already came
choices.why: It only sees responses received after it started listening; one that arrived earlier is gone.

choices.text: It misses the answer and times out
choices.why: Right. That is why the promise is created before the action and awaited after it.

choices.text: Playwright queues the response until a wait asks for it
choices.why: There is no such queue; that is the whole reason for starting the wait first.

choices.text: Nothing different; a fast server only makes it pass sooner
choices.why: A fast server is the case that breaks it, because the answer beats the listener.

prompt: A page shows a `.spinner` while a request is out, but adds it 200 ms after the last key, when its own delay ends. A test types, then waits for `.spinner` to be hidden, then reads the rows. What is the weakness?

choices.text: A spinner is not an accessible element
choices.why: Whether it is announced does not change when it appears, which is the problem here.

choices.text: Hidden is checked once and never retried
choices.why: A web-first wait retries; it simply has nothing to wait for when the condition is already true.

choices.text: The condition holds before the page starts work
choices.why: Right. The condition is true before the page has started working, so the wait passes at once and reads the old rows.

choices.text: Two hundred milliseconds is too short to be seen
choices.why: Playwright checks the DOM, not a person's eye; the trouble is that it is satisfied too early.

prompt: The shop's server is slowed so that `/api/products` answers after 6 seconds. The smoke test's `await expect(page.locator('#products li')).toHaveCount(8)` runs with Playwright's defaults. What is the verdict?

choices.text: It passes, since the assertion retries until the list fills
choices.why: It retries only for its timeout, five seconds by default, and the answer comes a second later.

choices.text: It fails with 0 found after five seconds
choices.why: Right. A web-first assertion waits as long as its timeout allows and no longer.

choices.text: It fails at once, because `goto` returned to an empty list
choices.why: An empty list at `goto` is what the assertion's retrying is for; it does not fail at the first look.

choices.text: `goto` waits the six seconds for the products
choices.why: `goto` waits for the `load` event, which does not include requests a script makes afterwards.

prompt: Suppose `/api/offer` sent `Cache-Control: no-cache` and no `ETag`. On a returning customer's second visit, what would the offer request get?

choices.text: A `304`, so the old offer is shown again
choices.why: A `304` needs a fingerprint to compare; with none, the server cannot say the copy is still good.

choices.text: The kept copy, unasked, for ten minutes
choices.why: That is what `max-age=600` allows; `no-cache` makes the browser ask before every use.

choices.text: A `200` with the new offer from the server
choices.why: Right. The browser must ask, and with no fingerprint to quote the server sends the whole answer.

choices.text: Nothing; `no-cache` forbids the request
choices.why: `no-cache` forbids using a copy unchecked; it never forbids asking.

prompt: A site serves `/style.css`, a name that never changes, with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000`. A release changes the stylesheet. What do returning visitors see?

choices.text: The new stylesheet, since the server's file changed
choices.why: The browser was told it need not ask for a year, so it never learns the file changed.

choices.text: The new one, after a `304` check
choices.why: With `max-age` there is no check until the age runs out, and a `304` would mean unchanged anyway.

choices.text: The old one, possibly for up to a year
choices.why: Right. A long `max-age` is safe only for names that change with their content, like `app.3f9c1a.js`.

choices.text: A broken page, because the copy no longer matches
choices.why: Nothing compares the copy with the server; the old stylesheet is used as if it were current.

prompt: A test must imitate a customer who closes the browser tonight and opens it again tomorrow, cache included. Which tool from the course does that?

choices.text: A new context built from a saved `storageState`
choices.why: `storageState` carries cookies and local storage and not the HTTP cache; that visitor saw the new offer.

choices.text: `launchPersistentContext`, with a folder
choices.why: Right. It writes the cache to the folder, and the second launch reads it back.

choices.text: A new page opened with `browser.newPage()`
choices.why: That makes a fresh context with an empty cache: a first visit.

choices.text: The `request` fixture, sent twice
choices.why: `request` has no cache of any kind; it always sees what the server says now.

prompt: A colleague opens a DevTools Protocol session and sends only `Network.setCacheDisabled` with `cacheDisabled: true`. On Chromium 141, what did the course see when that was tried?

choices.text: An error naming the missing `Network.enable`
choices.why: Nothing complained; that is what makes the missing line dangerous.

choices.text: The cache went off, so the new offer appeared
choices.why: That happened only with `Network.enable` sent first.

choices.text: The old offer, and no complaint
choices.why: Right. Without `Network.enable` the setting did nothing, silently.

choices.text: The page reloaded with every request uncached
choices.why: The command reloads nothing, and here it changed nothing either.

prompt: A suite adds `await page.route('**/api/**', r => r.continue())` in a `beforeEach`, to log calls. Which of its tests stops being able to find the stale offer?

choices.text: Only tests that use the `request` fixture
choices.why: `request` never had a cache to lose; the route acts on the page.

choices.text: None; a route that changes nothing changes nothing
choices.why: The course's `routing hides the flaw` test is exactly that route, and it passed.

choices.text: Only a test that checks the `Cache-Control` header
choices.why: A header test reads the server's answer and is unaffected by routing the page.

choices.text: The returning-customer test
choices.why: Right. Enabling routing disables the HTTP cache for that page, so the second visit asks the server.

prompt: A test written for a multi-page site clicks a link and then calls `await page.waitForLoadState()`. Ported to the SPA at `/spa/`, what does that line do after a click on **Basket**?

choices.text: It returns at once, since nothing loads
choices.why: Right. `load` fired once when `/spa/` opened, and `pushState` fires no other.

choices.text: It waits until the basket's fetch has answered
choices.why: A load state knows about documents, not about requests a script makes.

choices.text: It waits for the new document to arrive
choices.why: There is no new document; the click asked the server only for `/api/basket`.

choices.text: It throws, because the address changed
choices.why: Changing the address with `pushState` is an ordinary event for the page and raises nothing.

prompt: The developers add a real fallback: every unknown address under `/spa/` is answered with the app's page. A test opens `/spa/nonsense` and expects `response.status()` to be 404. What happens?

choices.text: It passes; the server still knows the address is unknown
choices.why: With a fallback, the server no longer tells unknown addresses apart: it sends the page.

choices.text: It fails: the status is 200 now
choices.why: Right. Only the app's own `Not found` view says it, so the suite has to check that view instead.

choices.text: It passes once `test.fail()` is removed
choices.why: Removing the mark does not change what the server answers.

choices.text: It fails, because the service worker answers it
choices.why: In a new context there is no worker installed; the server answered.

prompt: To stop returning visitors running an old app, a developer makes the server send `Cache-Control: no-store` on `/spa/spa.js`. The worker is unchanged. What does a visitor who was here yesterday get?

choices.text: The new script, since nothing may be stored
choices.why: The header governs the HTTP cache; the worker's copy is in Cache Storage and is read first.

choices.text: A `304` from the server, then the new script
choices.why: The server is not asked at all; the worker answers from its copy.

choices.text: An error, since the copy breaks the new header
choices.why: Nothing compares the worker's copy with any header; it is served as it is.

choices.text: The old script, from the worker's copy
choices.why: Right. `caches.match` reads no header and checks with nobody, so the change has to reach the worker itself.

prompt: A tester wants to catch the stale shell before release. Put the steps in order.
items: open the site on the old build, in a kept profile
open the site again in the same profile
trap: A fresh profile at any step gives a first visit, and a first visit always gets the new build.

prompt: Suppose the worker also answered `/api/products` cache first. The shop changes a price on the server. What does a returning visitor see?

choices.text: The new price, since data always goes to the server
choices.why: Only this worker's rule sends `/api/` to the network; change the rule and the data is cached too.

choices.text: The old price, from the worker's copy
choices.why: Right. Cache first answers from the copy whenever one exists, and nothing ever replaces it.

choices.text: An empty list, as in the offline test
choices.why: The list was empty offline because the data was not cached; here it would be.

choices.text: A 404, since the worker has no route
choices.why: A worker answers from its cache by the request; it needs no server route.

prompt: A page asks the server for news every two seconds. A test waits with `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` before checking a headline. What happens?

choices.text: It waits half a second and goes on
choices.why: It needs half a second with no request, and this page never gives one.

choices.text: It returns once the first news answer arrives
choices.why: `networkidle` is about the network going quiet, not about one response.

choices.text: It never sees the network quiet, and times out
choices.why: Right. A page that keeps asking never goes quiet, which is one reason the documentation discourages it for tests.

choices.text: It passes, since polling is not a page load
choices.why: Every request counts against idleness, whoever made it.

prompt: Suppose `/slow/ssr.js` were held back 6000 ms instead of 1500. The test waits with `await expect(page.locator('body')).toHaveAttribute('data-ready', 'true')` on Playwright's defaults. What is the verdict?

choices.text: It fails after five seconds, before the marker is set
choices.why: Right. The assertion retries for its five-second timeout and the script arrives a second later.

choices.text: It passes after six seconds
choices.why: It would, with a longer timeout; the default gives up at five.

choices.text: It passes at once, as `toBeEnabled` did
choices.why: The marker is absent until `ssr.js` runs; that is why it is a good signal.

choices.text: `goto` waits the six seconds, then it passes
choices.why: The script is asked for after `load`, so `goto` has already returned.

prompt: The page adopts the fix: buttons are sent `disabled` and enabled by `ssr.js`. A test with `javaScriptEnabled: false` clicks Banana's button. What does Playwright do?

choices.text: It clicks, and the basket says 0
choices.why: A disabled button fails the actionability checks, so the click is not performed.

choices.text: It refuses at once with a strict mode violation
choices.why: Strict mode is about a locator matching more than one element; this one matches one.

choices.text: It waits, until the test times out
choices.why: Right. No script runs to enable it, so the actionability wait never ends on its own.

choices.text: It runs `ssr.js` itself so the button works
choices.why: With JavaScript off in the context, no page script runs, and Playwright does not run one for it.

prompt: A team wants to check that every product's name is in the HTML a crawler receives from `/ssr`, a crawler that runs no script. Which check fits best?

choices.text: A browser test waiting for `data-ready`
choices.why: That checks the page after a script ran, which is not what the crawler gets.

choices.text: A `request` test reading the HTML
choices.why: Right. It sees exactly what anything without JavaScript sees, faster than a browser.

choices.text: A browser test of `/` with `javaScriptEnabled: false`
choices.why: That checks the other page, the one whose HTML holds no products at all.

choices.text: A smoke test counting cards with `toHaveCount(8)`
choices.why: In a browser the count includes what scripts drew, so it says nothing about the HTML.

prompt: A stylesheet changes the layout with `@media (min-width: 768px)`. Which pair of widths tests the line itself?

choices.why: `min-width: 768px` means 768 or wider, so both of these get the same layout.
Right. 767 is the last width without the rule and 768 the first with it, the mirror of 600 and 601 for `max-width`.
Those are the two ends; they check two layouts and not the line between them.
That is the line of the shop's own `max-width: 600px`, not of this rule.

prompt: Suppose `.basket` had `min-width: 22rem` instead of `24rem`. By the lesson's arithmetic, 16 pixels to a rem plus the header's 1rem of padding on the left, how wide would the page be in a window 360 pixels wide?
A team tests `/deals` in desktop Chromium windows 360, 600, 601 and 1280 pixels wide, and every test passes. What have they learnt about the page phones get?

choices.text: That phones get it at 360 and below
choices.why: The server never learns the window's width; a 360-pixel desktop window still asks as a desktop.

choices.text: That the breakpoints work on both sides
choices.why: Breakpoints are a stylesheet's; this page is chosen on the server by its `User-Agent`.

choices.text: Nothing: all four got the desktop page
choices.why: Right. An adaptive page is picked from the `User-Agent`, so only a device's name, not a width, reaches the other page.

choices.text: That `Vary: User-Agent` is set correctly
choices.why: None of these tests read the header, and a width says nothing about it.

prompt: A new page of the shop has no viewport tag. A test in a desktop window 390 wide sees its phone layout drawn correctly. What does an iPhone show?

choices.text: The same phone layout, at 390 wide
choices.why: A phone honours the tag and its absence; without it the window it reports is not narrow.

choices.text: A layout about 980 wide, shrunk
choices.why: Right. With no tag the phone falls back to a desktop-sized window, so no narrow-window rule applies, as on `/deals`.

choices.text: A page that scrolls sideways by 40 pixels
choices.why: That was the `.basket` flaw on a page that has the tag.

choices.text: A blank page, since the browser refuses it
choices.why: Browsers draw pages without the tag; they draw them as if for a desktop.

prompt: A test runs in Chromium with the iPhone 13 descriptor, minus its `defaultBrowserType`. What does that test get from the descriptor? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The iPhone's `User-Agent` string
choices.why: Right. A server reading the name sees an iPhone, which is why `/deals` sent the phone page.

choices.text: Touch, and `(pointer: coarse)` answering yes
choices.why: Right. `hasTouch` sets both, and `viewport.mjs` measured `touch: true`.

choices.text: WebKit's way of laying out and painting
choices.why: The engine is still Chromium; only a WebKit run would show WebKit's behaviour.

choices.text: A device pixel ratio of 3
choices.why: Right. `deviceScaleFactor: 3` is one of the six options it sets.

choices.text: The phone's processor, memory and network
choices.why: Emulation sets what the page can ask about; it does not slow the machine down to a phone.

prompt: A Selenium suite is moved from Chrome to Edge by changing `forBrowser('chrome')` to `forBrowser('MicrosoftEdge')`. What has to exist for a session to open?

choices.text: Nothing new; `chromedriver` drives every Chromium browser
choices.why: Each browser has its own driver from its own maker; Edge's is Microsoft's.

choices.text: A Selenium Grid with an Edge node
choices.why: A grid is optional; a local driver is enough.

choices.text: An `msedgedriver` whose major version is Edge's
choices.why: Right. The rule for `chromedriver` holds for `msedgedriver`, and Selenium Manager can fetch the right one.

choices.text: `geckodriver`, the standard's reference driver
choices.why: `geckodriver` is Mozilla's, for Firefox; the standard has no reference driver.

prompt: Chrome updated itself to 143 overnight. Selenium Manager's cache holds `chromedriver` 143, and a forgotten `chromedriver` 141 sits on the `PATH`. What happens when the suite starts?

choices.text: Selenium Manager picks 143, which fits
choices.why: It looks on the `PATH` first and uses what it finds there, even when it does not fit.

choices.text: The tests run, with a warning that 141 is untested
choices.why: Two versions behind is not the forgiving case; lesson 8's 139 against 141 failed outright.

choices.text: Session not created; delete the old driver on the `PATH`
choices.why: Right. The driver on the `PATH` is used and refuses the newer Chrome; removing it lets Selenium Manager supply one that fits.

choices.text: Chrome rolls back to 141 to match
choices.why: Nothing in Selenium changes the installed browser's version.

prompt: A Selenium session has an implicit wait of 3000 ms. On a page with neither, a test checks that no `.error` exists and then that no `.warning` exists, each with one `findElements`. Roughly how many milliseconds do the two checks take together?
A grid node's log says `Adding Firefox for {"browserName": "firefox"} 4 times`, and no Firefox is installed on that machine. What does that show?

choices.text: A slot is a promise the node makes, not a browser anybody checked
choices.why: Right. The node offered Firefox because it could not check without the internet; a request for it would fail on that node.

choices.text: The grid downloads Firefox when a test asks for it
choices.why: Nothing in that run downloaded a browser; it was offline and offered the slots anyway.

choices.text: Firefox sessions are routed to Chromium instead
choices.why: The distributor matches capabilities; it does not swap one browser for another.

choices.text: Standalone mode runs Firefox inside Java
choices.why: The grid is a Java program; the browsers it drives are separate programs.

prompt: A test asks a Selenium Grid for a new Chrome session. Put what happens inside the grid in order.
items: the distributor hands it to a node with a matching slot
trap: The distributor cannot choose a node before the request has been queued, and the node starts nothing until it is given a request.

prompt: Inside `cy.origin('http://127.0.0.1:3000', () => { ... })`, a test uses a variable `fruit` declared earlier in the test. What happens?

choices.text: It works, as any JavaScript closure does
choices.why: The function is sent to the other origin as text, so the closure does not travel with it.

choices.text: Cypress copies every variable across by itself
choices.why: Nothing is copied unless the test passes it in.

choices.text: The browser blocks it with a `SecurityError`
choices.why: That error is for a script reading a cross-origin frame; here the variable simply is not there.

choices.text: It is not there; pass it in with the `args` option
choices.why: Right. The function runs in that origin from its text, and a value it needs comes through `args`.

prompt: A Cypress test stubs `/api/products` with `delay: 6000`, then checks `cy.get('#products li').should('have.length', 1)` with no `cy.wait`. `defaultCommandTimeout` is untouched. What happens?

choices.text: It passes after six seconds
choices.why: The `should` retries only for its timeout, which the type definitions give as 4000 ms.

choices.text: It fails after about four seconds
choices.why: Right. The retry gives up at 4000 ms, two seconds before the stub answers; waiting on the route by name would have covered it.

choices.text: It fails at once, since the list starts empty
choices.why: A `should` is retried; an empty first look is what the retry is for.

choices.text: `cy.visit` waits for the stubbed answer
choices.why: The request is made by `app.js` after the page loads, and the visit does not wait for it.

prompt: A test must show two customers, each in a browser of their own, adding to the shop at the same moment. Which tool from the course can do it in one test?

choices.text: Cypress, with `cy.origin` for the second
choices.why: `cy.origin` moves the one tab to another origin; it does not open a second browser.

choices.text: Cypress, with two `describe` blocks
choices.why: Two groups run one after another in the same tab; they are never two people at once.

choices.text: Playwright, with two browser contexts
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10's test did exactly this, and showed both shoppers sharing the one basket.

choices.text: Either, since both run the test outside the page
choices.why: Cypress runs inside the page, which is why a second tab or browser is out of its reach.

prompt: A Cypress test stubs `/api/products` with status 500 and the text body `oops`, to check the page's error banner. The banner check would pass, yet the test fails. Why?

choices.text: A stub cannot return a status other than 200
choices.why: `cy.intercept` can answer with any status; that is one of the things it is for.

choices.text: `app.js` throws, and Cypress fails on it
choices.why: Right. Cypress fails a test on an uncaught application error, whatever the test checks, as lesson 1's stronger position asked.

choices.text: The real server answered before the stub did
choices.why: A route with an answer attached never reaches the real server.

choices.text: The banner is in another origin's frame
choices.why: The banner would be on the shop's own page, in the same origin as the test.

prompt: An assertion fails, and its call log says `9 × locator resolved to 0` and `unexpected value "0"`. What does that point at first?

choices.text: A locator that matches nothing
choices.why: That log would only ever say *waiting for*; this one found the element nine times.

choices.text: A strict mode violation
choices.why: Strict mode reports how many elements matched; this locator matched one.

choices.text: The page, not the locator
choices.why: Right. The element was there and held the wrong value, which is a question about the page.

choices.text: The test's 30 seconds running out
choices.why: This is the assertion's own clock of five seconds, reporting what it saw.

prompt: A trace of a failing test on a staging site with real accounts is attached to a public issue. What is the problem?

choices.text: Traces open only on the machine that made them
choices.why: A trace is a zip anybody can open, which is the problem here.

choices.text: It holds the pages and the request bodies
choices.why: Right. The screenshots and the network files carry whatever the pages showed and the requests sent.

choices.text: A trace is too large for an issue tracker
choices.why: The two-shopper trace was about 340 KB; size is not the risk.

choices.text: It shows only the test's source, which is private
choices.why: It holds the source and much more: screenshots, responses and the console.

prompt: In the two-shoppers test, suppose Bia had added an acerola instead of a mango. After Ana reloads, what total, in cents, does her basket hold?
A tester saw a defect in the Firefox she browses with, and installs Playwright's Firefox with `npx playwright install firefox` to reproduce it. Which browser will her tests drive?

choices.text: Her own Firefox, through `geckodriver`
choices.why: Playwright uses no driver program and does not drive the installed Firefox.

choices.text: Firefox's newest release, whatever she has
choices.why: Each Playwright version looks for one build, `firefox-1495` for 1.56.0.

choices.text: A modified build made for the tool
choices.why: Right. It is a Firefox extended with a protocol Playwright drives, so a defect in hers may or may not show there.

choices.text: Chromium, since only Chromium speaks CDP
choices.why: Firefox does not speak CDP, which is why Playwright ships a build of its own.

prompt: `tests/responsive.spec.js` holds 7 tests and `tests/deals.spec.js` holds 2. How many tests does `npx playwright test --config browsers.config.js --list` list for those two files?
Match each tool to what drives the browser underneath it.
A jsdom test measures lesson 7's targets with `getBoundingClientRect()` to check that each is 24 by 24 pixels. What will it find?

choices.text: The same sizes Chromium measured
choices.why: jsdom lays nothing out, so it has no sizes to agree with.

choices.text: Sizes in device pixels, three times larger
choices.why: There are no pixels of any kind without layout.

choices.text: An error, since the method does not exist
choices.why: The method exists and answers; what it answers is the trouble.

choices.text: No real size: nothing in jsdom is laid out
choices.why: Right. With no layout, nothing has a size or position, so the check cannot mean anything there.

prompt: A team's Nightwatch suite fails the morning after Chrome updated itself, with `This version of ChromeDriver only supports Chrome version 141`. Does lesson 8's advice apply?

choices.text: No; Nightwatch has its own protocol
choices.why: It speaks the W3C WebDriver API, the same protocol Selenium speaks.

choices.text: Yes: it runs on Selenium
choices.why: Right. Nightwatch depends on `selenium-webdriver`, so the fix is a driver that matches the browser.

choices.text: No; BrowserStack keeps its drivers current
choices.why: That holds for BrowserStack's own machines, not for the driver on this one.

choices.text: Only if the suite runs inside Jest
choices.why: Nightwatch brings its own runner; Jest has nothing to do with the driver.

prompt: A Puppeteer script is pointed at Firefox instead of Chrome. Which protocol does it speak there?

choices.text: The Chrome DevTools Protocol, as with Chrome
choices.why: Only Chromium-based browsers speak CDP.

choices.text: Classic WebDriver, through `geckodriver`
choices.why: Puppeteer does not use the one-request-one-answer protocol.

choices.text: Playwright's patched protocol
choices.why: That belongs to Playwright's own builds of Firefox.

choices.text: WebDriver BiDi
choices.why: Right. Its README names it: CDP for Chrome, WebDriver BiDi for Firefox.

prompt: Could `ProductCard`, built from a root locator, describe each result of lesson 3's search page, an `<li>` holding only the fruit's name?

choices.text: Yes; a component works on any page
choices.why: It works on any page that draws the same part; a result has no heading, price or button.

choices.text: No: the markup differs
choices.why: Right. The home page and `/ssr` share the card's markup; a search result is a different part and wants a class of its own.

choices.text: Yes, once it inherits from a `BasePage`
choices.why: Inheritance adds methods; it does not give the result the elements the card's locators look for.

choices.text: No, because locators cannot start from an `<li>`
choices.why: Any locator can be a root; the card itself is an `<li>`.

prompt: A file has ten tests and two of them need the shop open with an empty basket. The setup is in a `beforeEach`. What changes for the other eight if it becomes a `shop` fixture that only those two name?

choices.text: They stop paying for a reset and a page load
choices.why: Right. A fixture is built only for a test that names it, as the card tests showed.

choices.text: They get the fixture anyway, from the file
choices.why: That is how a `beforeEach` behaves; a fixture is set up on demand.

choices.text: They lose their `page` fixture
choices.why: `page` is built-in and still available to any test that names it.

choices.text: They must import `test` from `@playwright/test` instead
choices.why: Either import works for them; a test that never names `shop` never builds it.

prompt: A test needs the basket's count as a number, to check that adding a mango makes it one more than before. When is a page object method that returns the number honest?

choices.text: Never; a page object hands back only locators
choices.why: The rule is narrower: a value is fine once the page is settled.

choices.text: Any time, since it reads the DOM directly
choices.why: A read straight after a click returned 0 five times in five.

choices.text: Once an assertion has shown the page is finished
choices.why: Right. Read the value after a retrying assertion has settled it, as Cypress's `.then()` did in lesson 9.

choices.text: Only inside `expect.poll`, never elsewhere
choices.why: Polling is one way to wait; a settled page is the other, and then one read is enough.

prompt: A colleague adds a fixture `shopWithBananaInBasket` for the test that checks the count says 1 after a banana is added. What is the objection?

choices.text: Fixtures cannot click on a page
choices.why: A fixture can do anything a test can; the objection is about where the step belongs.

choices.text: The name is too long for Playwright
choices.why: Playwright accepts it; the trouble is what the name hides.

choices.text: It runs for every test in the suite
choices.why: A fixture runs only for tests that name it.

choices.text: It hides the step under test
choices.why: Right. Adding the banana is the subject, so it belongs in the test; a fixture prepares the world it starts in.

prompt: A Selenium `driver.wait` with the default poll interval is waiting for a condition that becomes true 1050 ms after the wait began. Ignoring how long each check takes, at how many milliseconds does the wait first see it true?
With Playwright's defaults, a test calls `page.goto` on an address whose `load` event never fires. What does the failure open with?

choices.text: `page.goto: Timeout 5000ms exceeded`
choices.why: Five seconds is the assertion's clock; a navigation has none of its own by default.

choices.text: `Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded`
choices.why: Right. `navigationTimeout` defaults to 0, no limit of its own, so the test's 30 seconds run out first.

choices.text: Nothing; the test waits until the job is killed
choices.why: 0 means no limit of its own, not no limit at all; the test's clock still runs.

choices.text: `webServer` timeout after 60 seconds
choices.why: That clock covers starting the shop, which had already started.

prompt: A test wraps a check of a server value in `await expect(async () => { ... }).toPass()`, with no options, and the value never matches. With the defaults, how long does it try?

choices.text: Five seconds, like any assertion
choices.why: `toPass` has no timeout of its own; its default in the installed code is 0.

choices.text: Once, since `toPass` does not retry
choices.why: Retrying the block until it stops throwing is what `toPass` is for.

choices.text: Until the test's 30 seconds run out
choices.why: Right. Without `{ timeout }` the outer clock decides, which is why the course always gives one.

choices.text: Two hundred milliseconds, then one more try
choices.why: 200 ms is Selenium's poll interval, not anything in `toPass`.

prompt: After a click, a page shows *Copied!* for 1.5 s. A test clicks, then spends about 2 s polling the server to confirm the copy, then expects *Copied!* with a 10-second timeout. It fails. What fixes it?

choices.text: A 30-second timeout on the message
choices.why: The message is gone before the assertion starts; a longer wait only watches an empty element longer.

choices.text: Checking the message first, straight after the click
choices.why: Right. Assert a fleeting state immediately after its cause, and leave the lasting state for later.

choices.text: A `waitForTimeout(1500)` before the message
choices.why: Any pause before the check makes it later, and later is the problem.

choices.text: Running the test with `--retries 2`
choices.why: Every attempt keeps the same order, so every attempt arrives after the message has gone.

prompt: A test truly fails one attempt in ten. In what percentage of runs of ten attempts would all ten pass anyway? Round to a whole number.
Match each flaky test to its cause.

pairs.left: Passes alone; fails when another worker empties the same table at that moment
Fails only when it runs after a test that left a row behind
Fails on the build machine, whose fonts make a label wrap
Draws a random quantity, and only the large ones fail

prompt: A run with `--retries 2` over twenty attempts ends with `1 failed`, `2 flaky`, `17 passed`. How many of the twenty needed at least one retry?
A project's quarantine folder holds fourteen tests. None names an owner or a date, and the oldest was moved there a year ago. What has the quarantine become?

choices.text: A safe place, since the tests still run
choices.why: They run and nobody reads them, so the defects they found stay where they are.

choices.text: A gate of its own that blocks releases
choices.why: A quarantine's result decides nothing; that is why it needs an owner and a date.

choices.text: A deletion done slowly
choices.why: Right. With no owner and no date, nobody brings a test back and the quarantine only grows.

choices.text: Proof that the suite has no flaky tests left
choices.why: It is fourteen flaky tests moved out of sight, not fourteen fixed.

prompt: Two basket tests run with `--fully-parallel --workers 2`. Each resets the shop first; then one adds a papaya and the other adds two mangoes, and both resets land before any click. What total, in cents, does the basket hold at the end?
A tester finds what look like real customers' names and CPFs in the staging users table. What should the defect report contain?

choices.text: A sentence, and no sample
choices.why: Right. Pasting a record as proof makes one more copy of somebody's data.

choices.text: Three rows, so the developers can find them
choices.why: The rows are the problem; quoting them spreads it into the report.

choices.text: A screenshot of the table, blurred
choices.why: A screenshot is still a copy, and a blur is not anonymisation.

choices.text: Nothing; staging is internal, so it is fine
choices.why: Test environments are less protected than production, and the law follows the data there.

prompt: A suite generates CPFs with valid check digits so that the form accepts them. What is the risk the lesson names?

choices.text: The form will reject them as duplicates
choices.why: Uniqueness is a separate question; the risk is whose number it is.

choices.text: Some valid numbers belong to real people
choices.why: Right. Prefer values the developers publish for tests, or a validation switched off in the test environment.

choices.text: Check digits make the tests slower
choices.why: The arithmetic costs nothing worth counting.

choices.text: Generated documents break the LGPD by themselves
choices.why: Made-up data is the recommended path; the danger is a made-up number that belongs to somebody.

prompt: A test creates the customer `cart-tester`, a fixed name, and deletes it in `afterEach`. A cancelled CI job kills the run with `SIGKILL` in the middle of it. Which change makes the next run pass anyway?

choices.text: Moving the delete into `afterAll`
choices.why: No hook runs after a `SIGKILL`; the workers are gone before any of them starts.

choices.text: A name made unique on every run
choices.why: Right. A leftover customer cannot collide with a name nobody has used, so the delete becomes tidy rather than essential.

choices.text: Two retries on the test
choices.why: The leftover customer is still there on every retry, so each one gets the same `409`.

choices.text: A longer timeout on the greeting
choices.why: *already exists* does not become *Welcome* by waiting.

prompt: In the search race's `0-trace.network`, the request for `?q=pa` started at `_monotonicTime` 2309.842 and its `time` was 602.719. At what time on the trace's clock did its answer arrive? Round to the nearest millisecond.
A visual test of a page that prints today's date in its header fails every morning. Which option stops the date from failing it, and at what price?

choices.text: `threshold`, and colour changes pass
choices.why: A threshold concerns how different one pixel's colour may be; a new date moves whole letters.

choices.text: `--update-snapshots` each morning, and nothing
choices.why: Updating daily accepts whatever the page drew, defects included.

choices.text: `mask` on the date, and nothing under it is checked
choices.why: Right. A mask paints over what changes by itself, and gives up checking that area.

choices.text: `maxDiffPixels: 0`, and the test runs slower
choices.why: Zero tolerance makes the comparison stricter, so the date fails it all the more.

prompt: A visual test goes red after a release. A colleague runs `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` and commits the new baselines without opening them. What has the suite accepted?

choices.text: Only the changes the release intended
choices.why: An update run cannot tell an intended change from a defect.

choices.text: Whatever the page drew, defects included
choices.why: Right. The new baseline is now the definition of correct, so a person has to look before it is committed.

choices.text: Nothing, until the build server approves it
choices.why: The baselines are files in the project; committing them is the approval.

choices.text: A tolerance of one percent on every picture
choices.why: Updating writes new pictures; it changes no tolerance.

prompt: The card-border change made 4794 of the 921,600 pixels differ. Had the test used `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01`, what would it have reported?

choices.text: A failure, since 0.01 is what the message printed
choices.why: The message rounds; the real ratio is about 0.005.

choices.text: A failure on every line of text
choices.why: That is a baseline compared on another machine; this one ran on the same.

choices.text: An error, because ratios need `threshold` too
choices.why: Each option stands on its own.

choices.text: A pass: about half a percent is under the tolerance
choices.why: Right. 4794 over 921,600 is about 0.005, so a change smaller than the tolerance passes, which is its price.

prompt: Match each value of the `trace` setting to what it records and keeps.

pairs.right: records every test, keeps the failures
records only the first retry of a failure

prompt: At 780 by 493, the Pineapple card's box had its top at 443.875 and a height of 133. How many pixels of it, to the nearest whole pixel, are below the bottom of the window?
Two CI jobs on one machine start `xvfb-run` at the same moment, and both ask for display 99. The option ___ makes each one look for a free display number instead.
A team adds a test of a browser extension. Their build server installed Chromium with `npx playwright install --only-shell chromium`. What will the test need?

choices.text: Nothing more; the shell is a full Chromium
choices.why: The shell is the old headless implementation, a separate and smaller program.

choices.text: The full Chromium, headed or with `channel: 'chromium'`
choices.why: Right. Extensions need the full browser, which `--only-shell` left out.

choices.text: `--headless=old` passed to the shell
choices.why: Old headless was removed from Chrome 141; asking for it fails.

choices.text: WebKit, which ships extension support
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson ties extensions to WebKit; they need the full Chromium.

prompt: A test checks that a page view reaches the site's analytics. It passes under `xvfb-run` with `--headed` and fails headless. Which explanation from the lesson fits?

choices.text: Headless skips running the page's scripts
choices.why: A headless browser parses, runs, lays out and paints exactly as a headed one.

choices.text: Headless pages are a different size
choices.why: Playwright's viewport is 1280 by 720 in every mode.

choices.text: Xvfb sends its own analytics events
choices.why: Xvfb draws windows into memory and nothing else.

choices.text: Its user agent says headless
choices.why: Right. Headless sends `HeadlessChrome`; under Xvfb the name was plain `Chrome`.

prompt: A Selenium test runs Chrome 141 with `--headless=new` and sets no window size. It expects the shop's **Menu** button, which shows at 600 pixels or narrower, to be visible. What happens?

choices.text: It passes; headless windows are phone-sized
choices.why: The window Chrome opened measured 780 wide, wider than the breakpoint.

choices.text: It fails: the 780-pixel window gets the wide layout
choices.why: Right. Selenium gives the page whatever window Chrome opens, which is why its suites set a size themselves.

choices.text: It passes, since Selenium sets 1280 by 720
choices.why: That viewport is Playwright's; Selenium sets none.

choices.text: It errors, since headless has no window at all
choices.why: Headless invents a window; it measured 780 by 441 here.

prompt: A page loads its pictures late with `IntersectionObserver`. A jsdom test opens it with scripts running. What does the course's run of jsdom 30.1.2 predict?

choices.text: The pictures load as the test scrolls
choices.why: There is no layout, so nothing scrolls into view, and the interface is missing anyway.

choices.text: The script throws on it
choices.why: Right. `IntersectionObserver` was `undefined`, so a page that calls it throws, as `app.js` did on `fetch`.

choices.text: Every picture loads at once
choices.why: jsdom does not fetch images without the extra `canvas` package, and the observer is missing.

choices.text: The same as Chromium, only faster
choices.why: This is a question about what is in view, which needs layout.

prompt: A Java team proposes HtmlUnit to test the SPA at `/spa/`, whose `spa.js` is written with `async` functions. What would its tests most likely report?

choices.text: The views drawn as in Chromium
choices.why: HtmlUnit's Rhino stopped at `async` on the shop's own scripts.

choices.text: The deep-link 404, as in lesson 5
choices.why: That is a server answer any client would see; it says nothing about the views.

choices.text: A script error and empty views, which no user meets
choices.why: Right. Rhino would not parse the script, so nothing draws: a difference between HtmlUnit and every user, not a defect.

choices.text: A stale shell from the service worker
choices.why: No script ran, so no worker was ever registered.

prompt: In the first timing run, ten pages took 729 ms in jsdom and 1643 ms in Chromium. How many milliseconds per page did jsdom save? Round to the nearest whole number.
In jsdom, `document.body.innerText` was `undefined`, because what it returns depends on what is visible. The property that ignores styles, ___ , was there.
A build machine has 7 logical processors. Neither the configuration nor the command line sets `workers`. By the rule in Playwright's installed code, how many workers can `npx playwright test` start?
Five test files, forty tests between them, run with `--workers 8 --fully-parallel` on a machine with sixteen threads. How many workers does the run use?

choices.text: Five, one for each file
choices.why: That is the default unit of work; `--fully-parallel` makes each test a unit of its own.

choices.text: Eight, the number allowed
choices.why: Right. Forty tests are enough to keep all eight busy once tests, not files, are handed out.

choices.text: Sixteen, one per thread
choices.why: `--workers` on the command line comes first and caps it at eight.

choices.text: Forty, one per test
choices.why: A worker runs one test after another; the count never goes past `--workers`.

prompt: A suite holds one file of forty tests and twenty files of one test each, none of them fully parallel. It runs as `--shard=1/3`, `2/3` and `3/3`. Why can the shards not come out even?

choices.text: Playwright deals shards by each file's last duration
choices.why: It does not know how long a test takes; `filterForShard` counts tests.

choices.text: Shards need a blob report to balance themselves
choices.why: A blob report only merges the results afterwards.

choices.text: The big file is never split, so one shard gets all forty
choices.why: Right. A group is a whole file unless it is fully parallel; marking it so lets its tests be dealt out apart.

choices.text: Three shards need a multiple of three files
choices.why: Any count of groups can be dealt; the trouble is one group holding most of the tests.

prompt: In the curve, peak memory was 924 MB with one worker and 4476 MB with eight. On average, how many megabytes did each worker added after the first cost? Round to the nearest whole number.
With the final `turns.config.js`, where `one-at-a-time` depends on `parallel`, a test in `parallel` fails. What happens to the shop's tests in `one-at-a-time`?

choices.text: They run as usual, after the failure
choices.why: A project whose dependencies did not all pass is left out of the run.

choices.text: They are left out, so nobody learns whether they pass
choices.why: Right. `tasks.js` drops it, which suits a sign-in setup project and is a nuisance here, where the two groups need nothing from each other.

choices.text: They run in parallel, to make up the time
choices.why: `workers: 1` on the project never changes because of another project's result.

choices.text: They are retried until `parallel` passes
choices.why: Nothing in a dependency waits for, or retries, the project it depends on.

prompt: Suppose each card's button carried `data-testid="add-banana"` and so on, spelt the shop's way. Going through Selenium IDE's builders in their order, which one names the banana's button first?

choices.text: `css:data-test-id`, which looks for test attributes
choices.why: It reads only `data-test-id` and `data-test`, not the shop's spelling.

choices.text: `css:data-attr`, the third in the order
choices.why: Right. The third builder takes the element's own first `data-*` attribute, as it did for the basket count.

choices.text: `css:finder`, with the card's random id
choices.why: The finder is fourth; a `data-*` attribute on the button is taken before it is reached.

choices.text: `xpath:innerText`, from the button's words
choices.why: The XPath builders come last, and an earlier one already answers.

prompt: A `.side` recording's `target` names a random card id that no longer exists, and its `targets` list also holds `xpath=//button[contains(.,'Add to basket')]`. What does the IDE's playback do?

choices.text: It tries the next entry in `targets` and clicks
choices.why: The loop that would try the alternatives is commented out in `side-runtime`.

choices.text: It asks the person to pick an entry, then goes on
choices.why: Playback asks nobody; choosing another entry is something a person does in the IDE afterwards.

choices.text: It waits for the target, then fails the step
choices.why: Right. A click polls for its target up to the implicit wait and fails; the list is kept for a person, not tried.

choices.text: It skips the step and marks it as a warning
choices.why: A step that cannot find its target fails, as `recorded/side.spec.js` did after five seconds.

prompt: An application marks its elements with `data-qa`. To make codegen build its test-id locators from that attribute, the option is `npx playwright codegen --___ data-qa`.

A team has 50 recorded flows, and each clicks *Add to basket* twice, with the full locator written on each line as codegen writes it. The button is renamed. How many lines name the old words and need editing?
At the 281 ms the browser test took, how many seconds would 500 such checks take on one worker, run 20 times a day?
A test fails one run in a hundred for reasons unrelated to the shop. In what percentage of series of 50 runs would it pass all 50? Round to a whole number.
A change keeps `total()` right but makes `POST /api/basket` answer `{ lines, sum: 590 }` instead of `total: 590`. Which of the lesson's three tests fail?

choices.text: Only the unit test of `total()`
choices.why: The function was not touched, so its three cases still pass.

choices.text: The API test and the browser test
choices.why: Right. The API test compares the whole answer, and the page reads `basket.total`, which is now missing.

choices.text: Only the browser test, as with the cents
choices.why: This time the API's own answer changed, and the API test checks it with `toEqual`.

choices.text: None, since the arithmetic is right
choices.why: Two of the tests check more than the arithmetic: the answer's shape and what the page draws.

prompt: The testing trophy's wide integration band renders components in jsdom. Which defect from this course would that band still miss?

choices.text: A price read wrongly from an API answer
choices.why: Reading data into the DOM is what jsdom does well; no layout is needed.

choices.text: A component that forgets to draw a heading
choices.why: A missing element is in the tree, and jsdom has the tree.

choices.text: Lesson 7's basket, too wide for a phone
choices.why: Right. jsdom has no layout and reported a `scrollWidth` of 0, which is why the trophy keeps a cup of end-to-end tests too.

choices.text: A handler wired to the wrong button
choices.why: jsdom runs listeners when an element is clicked, so a wrong wiring shows.

prompt: Which of these checks on quitanda have earned a place in the browser layer, by lesson 21's question? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Open the shop, add a banana and read the total
choices.why: Right. A journey crosses every seam at once, which is what the few tests at the top are for.

choices.text: The click on `/ssr` before its script has arrived
choices.why: Right. The HTML was right throughout; only a browser sees the buttons doing nothing.

choices.text: All 65,536 baskets of none to three of each fruit
choices.why: That is arithmetic, and a handful of unit cases with something to say covers it.

choices.text: Every name the server should refuse with `409`
choices.why: One browser test shows the refusal reaches the screen; the other cases belong to the layer that decides.

choices.text: The page that scrolls sideways at 360 pixels
choices.why: Right. Overflow is layout, and only something that lays the page out can measure it.

prompt: Keep the lesson's assumptions for the screenshot test, 10 minutes to write and 10 minutes for each change that breaks it, but say the shop's look changes once a quarter. What is its person cost for a year, in minutes?
Suppose a suite's declared failures cost 12.4 seconds a run, and the suite runs 5,000 times a year. How many minutes of machine time a year do they spend? Round to the nearest whole number.
A suite holds 100 tests, each failing one run in 200 for no reason, independently. Roughly what share of its runs go red with nothing changed?

choices.text: Half of one percent, like each test
choices.why: A developer meets a red run, and a run is red when any one of the hundred fails.

choices.text: About two in five
choices.why: Right. 1 − 0.995 to the power 100 is about 0.39, which is why the lesson tracks red runs, not red tests.

choices.text: Exactly half, since 100 is half of 200
choices.why: The chances do not add; each run is green only if all hundred pass.

choices.text: Every run, since one test always fails
choices.why: With 1 in 200 each, many runs still have no failure at all.

prompt: The search defect is fixed. Lesson 3's test and lesson 13's `waitForFunction` test both report *Expected to fail, but passed*. After removing both marks, what does the lesson ask?

choices.text: Keep both, since two checks are safer
choices.why: Two tests of one behaviour double the upkeep and catch nothing the first does not.

choices.text: Delete both, since the defect is gone
choices.why: The fix is now worth guarding; one of them becomes the regression check.

choices.text: Mark both with `test.skip()` until next month
choices.why: A skipped test stops looking, and nothing says when to start again.

choices.text: Keep the clearer one; give the reason in the commit
choices.why: Right. Keep the one whose failure would tell a developer more, and write why the other went.
